That is why certain snacks have to be made out of a mash and then shaped so they stack in transit. Finally, it isn't 'air', it's nitrogen. The nitrogen is there to keep freshness, which means they don't have to put more preservatives into the snacks.

Are you completely misinformed? Selective breeding involves choosing a unique or rare desirable trait in a species and breeding individuals with that trait to preserve it. While it is true that selective breeding in certain animals, like specific dog breeds and poultry, can be problematic, corgis are not the result of selective breeding in the same way. They are simply bred for their characteristics. The dwarfism seen in corgis is not unique to any individual dog; it is a trait of the breed as a whole. Not utilizing a corgi for their speed and short stature is akin to not using a dog for detection purposes. Are you suggesting we shouldn't do that?

Regarding a certain breed of cats, they were not truly selectively bred initially. A cat with that trait was born and produced more offspring. There may have been selective breeding afterward, but this is a relatively recent breed that was only recognized as a true breed in the last few years, and there is still some debate about it. Corgis, on the other hand, have a history that goes back over 400 years, and there was not much selective breeding occurring in that region of Wales at the time.

The main problem with a popular open-world game on one console was how the manufacturer set up the RAM. The company decided to split the 512MB of RAM into 256MB for processing and 256MB for video, similar to how a current computer has a dedicated video card. In contrast, another manufacturer simply allocated the full 512MB of RAM for general use.

The game developer, lacking foresight, built the game engine to utilize the full 512MB of the competing console and then attempted to adapt it to the 256MB of the other console. This approach proved ineffective and led to numerous issues with that version of the game.

Meanwhile, other developers learned to effectively utilize the dual memory system of the problematic console and created highly acclaimed games.

Now, the memory architecture of the latest generation of consoles is quite similar, so such issues are unlikely to arise in the future.

In summary, the game developer struggled with optimizing for the memory of the earlier console, but the newer generation does not have that limitation.

If she wants to heal and be combat effective, then do a search for builds focused on healing and support. Basically, you take 3 levels of a healing-focused class with a specific ability that allows you to link to a number of characters equal to your level, and then the rest as a warrior class. This ability allows you to automatically heal linked characters for a certain amount of damage at the beginning of your turn, while taking the same amount of damage yourself. This is where the warrior class levels come in, as you can quickly use a healing ability to recover the damage you took. Since it is a swift action, you can still use all of your other actions to cast spells or attack.

I would probably go with a small character type. 3 levels of the healing class and 5 levels of the warrior class. This gives you a special bond with a companion, and I would choose a dog. Then take a feat that enhances your companion. This means the dog is an effective higher-level companion, so it can be used indoors. Finally, emphasize ranged combat with your warrior class. Don't forget that your special attack works with ranged attacks.

Trust me, this is one of the best combat-effective healers out there.

I've backed 60. Yea, I know, I'm ~~addicted~~ hooked [or is that still too much for you]. The first thing you have to remember is that you probably are going to pay actually more than retail. With the advent of websites like online retailers and even major e-commerce platforms cutting their prices, you are going to pay more. So why do it? The main reason I do it is for exclusives and 'freebies' you get through the campaign. Unfortunately, you probably won't know what the whole package is until the last couple of days, so I mostly just mark one that looks interesting and then when I get the notice there are 48 hours left I do my final research.

What I look for in a campaign? First, the game has to excite me as something new. If it is something I already have on the shelf, then I will typically pass. Second, it HAS to have a copy of the rules for me to download and check over. I always look over the rules to get a rough idea about the game. Third, I really look for a gameplay video. I typically will not back something that doesn't show what the gameplay is like. Finally, I really like a third-party review. Now, I know most of these are paid, but I don't care. I like to see another set of eyes go over the game and give their opinion.

Okay, so the game has passed these tests, what else? I never back a project from someone that is doing their first crowdfunding campaign unless the campaign has been really well done. The biggest pain in the neck projects I've had have always been from creators that have a great idea but don't know what they are doing. I really check over the 'freebies'. If they aren't worth the extra cost of the pledge, then I'll pass and buy retail. Finally, I like to look over their responses to the comments. If they can't handle a little constructive criticism, then I might pass.

Finally, there are some companies that just get a pass on most of this and I pledge right away. I am totally hooked on their miniatures and have found most of their games to be fun if a little shallow.

On a side note, don't get hung up on when you are going to get your pledge. I bet 95% of pledges don't meet their goals. Almost always it is something to do with shipping or problems with the manufacturer. Those aren't going to go away. There are always going to be problems dealing with this, but those problems would have been there for the retail release anyways. Anyone that didn't back the campaign is going to have to wait those extra 6-8 months also, so when someone complains about how long a campaign is taking I just sort of laugh at them.

On that note, there is a limit. If it takes years like almost every digital game I have backed, then yeah, complaining is fine. I won't ever back another digital game. They take forever and it is so annoying.

P.S. I've only had 1 of those 60 games bail on the campaign. Fortunately for me, another company came in and completed the campaign for free and I still got my game. I didn't get the sweet metal miniatures I paid for, but at least I got what I think is a pretty cool game. Now, I did have 1 problem where a creator got in over his head and couldn't pay the postage, and I ended up sending him the postage to get the game, but that problem has been mostly solved with pretty much everyone charging shipping and handling after the campaign. I also have a couple of digital games I've been waiting on for some time. Neither has been canceled, but that is one of the reasons I don't do digital game crowdfunding.
